prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength are interrogated free of light shift, Doppler and recoil effects, and for its development to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: After the full first round my preferred configuration is unchanged: B012, Katori and Ye, as a single part. What has changed is how firmly I can answer the objections, because the chair's questions made me separate them. The physics is a single idea with a decisive consequence. At the magic wavelength the differential light shift of the two clock states vanishes, so a lattice can hold thousands of neutral atoms with Doppler and recoil shifts removed while all are interrogated together. That removes the old trade-off between atom number and systematic shifts and is what opened the 1e-18 regime. The evidence is quantitative and independently reproduced and compared (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL), which is the test I apply to any result I did not do myself. It is also not only an instrument: it has delivered relativistic redshift over millimetres, bounds on drifts of constants and new dark-matter searches. On the chair's question about credit, I will state it plainly. The magic-wavelength lattice concept and the first demonstration with strontium are Katori's. The record accuracy and stability, the many-body clock work in the lattice and the link to the frequency comb are Ye's, and without them the 1e-18 statement would not be established. Both roles are essential and they are distinct. Four other members (Kroll, Olsson, Pearce, Johansson) reach the same pair and the same wording, and I treat that as agreement on the facts, not as a count to lean on.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, the frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems including ion clocks) is the real weakness, and I do not think it can be argued away, only bounded. My bound is this: the comb is a ruler and the ion clock rests on control of one particle, whereas the lattice clock is a different way to reach the same precision by interrogating a large ensemble of neutral atoms in a trap whose perturbation is engineered to cancel. If the citation reads as a general award for better clocks, the objection becomes decisive for me. If it names the magic-wavelength lattice, it stays an answerable objection. A second weakness is priority. Lemonde, Pal'chikov, Takamoto and Ludlow all made early contributions, and a three-name limit cannot cover everyone. I think Takamoto is the most defensible addition as Katori's collaborator on the first demonstration, but that would change the structure of a clean pair and I do not think it is required. The SI second has not been redefined, which I treat as a consequence of the work and not a precondition. I also hold this view as an atomic physicist and have asked colleagues in other fields to test it.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B042 because a clean prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald) was followed by a decisive clue from nature, and notes that he would not be embarrassed if the committee chose B012 instead.
responses.response: I take this seriously and B042 remains my second choice, because I value an unexpected phase of matter appearing at a predicted angle. The sequence he describes is the right pattern. I still rank it below B012 for the reason he himself raises: after eight years the pairing mechanism is not settled. His statement treats that as a risk of looking hasty, and I think it goes further, because without the mechanism the committee cannot say whether the superconductivity is conventional or unconventional and hence what exactly was discovered. I would be more comfortable with B042 if the citation were limited to the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which his wording nearly does. My answer to his question is that I would rank B012 above B042 now, and I would expect a later year to favour B042 if the mechanism clears.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B042 as a theoretical prediction realised in a clean, gate-tunable material, accepts that the mechanism of superconductivity and twist-angle disorder are open, and concedes that optical lattice clocks would be the safer choice.
responses.response: His statement helped me because he separates the discovery from the mechanism question and asks whether the mechanism is a necessary part of it. My view is that it is not strictly necessary: a state of matter can be a discovery before it is understood, as with high-temperature superconductors. But there I would add that those cases took decades to be recognised and the recognition was not controversial about what had been found. In twisted bilayer graphene the sample-to-sample variation from twist-angle disorder still affects what is claimed about the insulators. That is a reproducibility issue in the discovery itself and not only in the interpretation, which is why I put the clock ahead. I agree with him that the attribution problem on B042 (Cao, Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, and the follow-up groups) is larger than on B012.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B012 with a citation framed on the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, not on clocks in general, and asks whether the first lattice demonstrations and the many-body clock work should be described separately.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and have kept it in my citation. On his second point, I think the two should not be split into separate citation clauses. The first demonstrations (Takamoto and Katori) and the later many-body and record-accuracy work (Ye) are one continuous development, and splitting them would only invite a claim that two prizes are being conflated. I prefer one sentence naming the invention and the development, and the credit split can be recorded in the committee's own background text. He is also right that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is the point on which the committee should decide in the open, and I say above where I would find it decisive.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B012 after reading the openings, noting its cross-field support and that the independent confirmation across six laboratories is what he always asks for, while saying he relies on the atomic-physics members for priority details.
responses.response: Since he asks for the priority details, I give them with the caveat that I am reasoning from the supplied material and from my own knowledge of the field. Lemonde and Wolf worked on a Sr lattice clock scheme at SYRTE and on the effect of the lattice on the clock transition, and Pal'chikov and Ovsiannikov contributed to the magic-wavelength calculations, but Katori brought the idea to a working clock and made the key demonstration of a lattice clock with trapped Sr. I would not displace Katori or Ye for any of them. Ye's role is central because he demonstrated that the lattice clock could reach and verify the 1e-18 level, and the comparisons which make the claim credible came mainly from his group's work and the independent laboratories that followed. I also agree with his decision on the IceCube candidate: with one name for a large collaboration, it cannot be settled this year.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B042 as a minimal, analytically tractable model that predicts a sharp non-obvious condition, and says a two-achievement prize with B012 would be impractical under the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree with the last point and I do not propose a combination of B012 and B042, since five names would exceed the limit and two half-prizes would weaken both citations. I also share his admiration for the Bistritzer-MacDonald model: it is exactly the type of simple model with a sharp prediction that I value as a theorist. Where I differ is that a good model and a first confirmation do not by themselves settle maturity. His own case_against lists the right worries, namely the unsettled pairing, Cao's role and Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto. If the committee decides to wait on B012 for the redefinition of the second, I would ask for the same patience on B042 for its mechanism, and that would favour neither.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that a citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I would regard a generic clock citation as a reason to withdraw support.
Whether Takamoto, Lemonde or Ludlow have a claim strong enough to change the credited pair. I think not, but I cannot verify the detailed history from the supplied material.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be awaited. I treat it as a consequence, but I cannot predict how colleagues will weigh it.
Whether the pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder in twisted bilayer graphene will be resolved in a way that makes B042 clearly the better choice in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged. I have a long-standing collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, the 2023 laureate, and co-authorship with the Lund and Keller attosecond groups, but none of them is credited on any shortlisted ballot. I have no connection to Katori, Ye or any other credited name that I know of. My field is close to B012, B019 and B020, and I have disclosed this proximity; the committee has seen five members reach B012 independently, including colleagues from other fields, which reduces my concern about over-weighting it.
